common_name: Red Potato Onion (Heirloom Red Multiplier Onion)
scientific_name: Allium cepa var. aggregatum 'Red Potato Onion'

planting.note: Plant small saved bulbs in fall in mild-winter areas for the largest bulbs the following summer, or in very early spring once soil is workable where winters are severe.

directions: Red Potato Onion is a coppery-red to purple-skinned heirloom multiplier onion maintained within the same potato-onion tradition as the better-known Yellow Potato Onion, propagated vegetatively from saved bulbs rather than seed. Each planted bulb splits underground into a cluster of several new bulbs by midsummer, giving gardeners a perpetual, pungent storage onion without annual seed purchases. It is notably drought tolerant once established and keeps well in storage over winter. Plant divisions about two inches deep with the tip near the soil surface, and replant the largest bulbs from each harvest to maintain vigor in the strain.

planting.note: Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost, then transplant into a trench once seedlings are pencil-thick, backfilling gradually to blanch the shafts as the plants grow.

directions: Bulgarian Giant is a traditional Eastern European leek grown for its thick, blue-green-topped shafts and outstanding cold hardiness, making it well suited to autumn and winter harvest after flavor has been sweetened by frost. The shanks can reach several inches in diameter under good growing conditions, with a milder, less pungent character than many summer leek types. Transplant into a deep trench or dibbled holes to maximize the length of blanched white shaft, hilling soil around the base as the plants size up. Harvest from fall through winter as needed, since mature plants hold well in the ground in cold weather rather than requiring immediate pulling.

common_name: Gladalan Brown Onion (Australian Heirloom Short-Day Storage Onion)

planting.note: In mild-winter regions sow directly in autumn so bulbs can begin forming as day length increases in spring; in colder climates sow as early as soil can be worked.

directions: Gladalan Brown is an early-to-midseason Australian heirloom storage onion developed in Western Australia in the early twentieth century and grown as a short-day type for mild-winter climates. It produces medium to large, firm, brown-skinned globes with a mild flavor that mellows further in cooking, and it has a reputation for keeping unusually well in storage. Because it is day-length sensitive, bulbing is triggered earliest in regions with shorter winter days, so gardeners outside its traditional short-day range should expect smaller bulbs. Thin direct-sown seedlings to their final spacing early to allow bulbs room to size up evenly.

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring; as a long-day type it needs the longer summer daylengths of northern latitudes to bulb well.

directions: Rijnsburger is a classic Dutch maincrop storage onion named for the bulb-growing region around Rijnsburg in the Netherlands, and it serves as the foundation strain behind many modern Dutch yellow storage onion selections still sold today. It forms large, uniform, globe-shaped bulbs with thin necks and a firm straw-to-bronze skin over crisp white flesh. Harvested bulbs cure well and are known for holding in storage from late summer harvest through the following winter and into early spring. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil with even moisture, and allow tops to fall over naturally before curing bulbs in a dry, airy spot.

common_name: Zittauer Gelbe Onion (Giant Zittau Yellow Storage Onion)

planting.note: Direct sow in spring as soon as the soil can be worked; this late-maturing type needs a full season to size up before fall harvest and curing.

directions: Zittauer Gelbe is a German heirloom onion dating to the nineteenth century, named for the town of Zittau and long popular in Central and Northern Europe as a reliable keeper. It forms firm, semi-globe bulbs with golden-brown skin and a notably strong, assertive onion flavor well suited to cooking rather than fresh eating. As a late-season type it needs a full growing season to reach full size, with harvest typically in late summer once tops begin to fall over. Cure bulbs thoroughly in a warm, airy location before moving them to cold storage, where they are reported to keep for many months.
